title: The Rational Root Theorem: the Candidate List

steps.body: Guessing zeros of a cubic feels hopeless — until the **Rational Root Theorem** shrinks the haystack: any rational zero p/q (in lowest terms) must have **p dividing the constant term** and **q dividing the leading coefficient**. The theorem doesn't find roots; it writes the complete **candidate list**.

widget.prompt: For f(x) = x³ + 2x² − 5x − 6, the candidates are ±(divisors of the constant). What is the constant term's absolute value?

commonErrors.feedback: 1 is the LEADING coefficient (of x³). The constant term — the number with no x — is −6, absolute value 6.
Use the absolute value for listing divisors: 6 (the ± signs are added afterward).

widget.fallbackFeedback: The constant term is −6; its divisors 1, 2, 3, 6 seed the candidate list.

explanationVariants: p ∈ {1, 2, 3, 6}, q ∈ {1}, with ± signs: ±1, ±2, ±3, ±6 — eight candidates.
Leading coefficient 1 means candidates are just the signed divisors of 6: four divisors × two signs = 8.

widget.prompt: f(x) = x³ + 2x² − 5x − 6 has leading coefficient 1 and constant −6. How many rational-root CANDIDATES are there?

commonErrors.feedback: Four divisors (1, 2, 3, 6) — but each carries BOTH signs: ±1, ±2, ±3, ±6 makes 8.
6 is the constant term itself. Count its signed divisors: ±1, ±2, ±3, ±6 → 8 candidates.

steps.body: A leading coefficient bigger than 1 adds **fractions**: q ranges over its divisors. For g(x) = 2x³ − 3x² − 3x + 2, p ∈ {1, 2} and q ∈ {1, 2}, so p/q gives ±1, ±2, ±1/2 (±2/2 repeats ±1). Always reduce and drop duplicates.

explanationVariants: p/q with p ∈ {1,2}, q ∈ {1,2}: ±1, ±2, ±1/2 after removing the duplicate 2/2 = 1 — six candidates.

widget.prompt: g(x) = 2x³ − 3x² − 3x + 2. After removing duplicates, how many DISTINCT rational-root candidates does the theorem give?

commonErrors.feedback: ±1, ±2, ±1/2, ±2/2 looks like 8, but 2/2 reduces to 1 — a duplicate. Six distinct values remain.
Don't forget the fractions: q = 2 adds ±1/2 beyond ±1 and ±2.

steps.body: What the theorem does NOT say.
explanationVariants: The theorem lists every POSSIBLE rational zero — it never promises any candidate actually works, and it says nothing about irrational or complex zeros.
It's a filter, not a guarantee: zeros like √2 or 1 + i sail past it entirely.

widget.prompt: Which statement about the Rational Root Theorem is true?

options.label: Every rational zero must appear on the list, but candidates can all fail
options.feedback: Right — it's a complete net for RATIONAL zeros only; a polynomial may have none.

options.label: At least one candidate is always a zero
options.feedback: x³ − 2 has candidates ±1, ±2, yet its real zero is ∛2 — irrational. Every candidate fails.

options.label: The list also catches irrational zeros
options.feedback: Irrational zeros like √2 are exactly what the theorem CAN'T see: it only constrains zeros of the form p/q.

steps.body: A list with two fraction layers.
explanationVariants: p ∈ {1, 5}, q ∈ {1, 3}: p/q ∈ {1, 5, 1/3, 5/3} with ± signs — eight distinct candidates (no duplicates arise).
Four positive values 1, 5, 1/3, 5/3, doubled by sign: 8.
hints: List p as the divisors of the constant 5, and q as the divisors of the leading 3.
p ∈ {1, 5}, q ∈ {1, 3}. Form every p/q, reduce, drop repeats.
1, 5, 1/3, 5/3 — none reduce to each other. Apply the ± signs.

widget.prompt: h(x) = 3x³ + x² − 5x + 5 (constant 5, leading 3). How many DISTINCT rational-root candidates are there?

commonErrors.feedback: 1, 5, 1/3, 5/3 is only the positive half — each also carries a minus sign: 8 total.
p has 2 divisors and q has 2, giving 4 positive ratios (×2 signs = 8) — 16 would double-count.

takeaways: Candidates are ±p/q: p | constant, q | leading coefficient.
The list is complete for rational zeros — but nothing on it is guaranteed.
steps.teaser: Next: putting candidates on trial — fast testing with the Factor Theorem.

concept.body: Two questions build the list: what divides the constant (that's p)? what divides the leading coefficient (that's q)? Candidates are every reduced ±p/q.

explanationVariants: Three divisors, two signs each: 6 candidates.

widget.prompt: f(x) = x³ − x − 4 (constant −4, leading 1). How many rational-root candidates are there?

commonErrors.feedback: 1, 2, 4 are the divisors — each gets BOTH signs: ±1, ±2, ±4 → 6.
4 is the constant's size. Its divisors 1, 2, 4 with signs give 6 candidates.
